content.title: Non-Smoker with Stage 4 Lung Cancer Was Given a Year to Live. That Was 7 Years Ago (Exclusive)
content.text: NEED TO KNOW Non-smoker Dave Nitsche was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer despite never smoking or having a family history of cancerHe has surpassed his initial prognosis by six years, thanks to targeted therapies and continuing to stay activeNitsche leads a cancer support group and plans to complete a 1,000-km bike ride in June Dave Nitsche liked to keep busy. The Winnipeg, Canada, native was an avid marathon runner, Ironman competitor and cyclist. But in March 2019, he noticed something strange with his vision. "I'd be looking at telephone poles or something, they would seem wavy," Nitsche, now 57, tells PEOPLE exclusively. He called his eye doctor, who suspected a detached retina — but after some ultrasounds and other tests, doctors discovered fluid behind his eye. Dave Nitsche is preparing for a 1000-km bike ride in June. Courtesy Dave Nitsche From there, things moved quickly, as doctors realized his eye couldn't be saved: "I had my eye removed two days before my 50th birthday, which was a wonderful birthday present," he quips. He was referred for more tests, including bone marrow scans and CT scans. After doctors found spots on his lungs, he visited a lung specialist who drained 1.5 liters of fluid from his lung. Three weeks after Nitsche's eye was removed, and two months after his vision began to change, Nitsche had an appointment with another doctor. "I went to the oncologist and he sat me down and says, 'You have fourth stage lung cancer.' " He was shocked. "I'd been feeling great," he says. Related Stories Nitsche had never smoked, and had no family history of lung cancer. He would sometimes experience a "little bit of back pain" after running, but figured it was "kind of normal." He was given a year to live — two at max. Nitsche began a targeted medication immediately to slow cancer growth. Then Nitsche hit the one-year mark of his prognosis. Then two years. "It was a bit of a celebration, for sure," he says. "You do appreciate the little things a bit more." Dave Nitsche said he hopes to clear up misconceptions about living with cancer. Courtesy Dave Nitsche After his targeted therapy became less effective, about a year ago, he switched to Rybrevant, which targets the main growth signals of a cancer cell, as well as another growth pathway. He gets the infusions every three weeks. "The tumors are getting smaller or becoming more like scar tissue," Nitsche explains, sharing that his oncologist showed him a CT scan, where he could see that "they're getting smaller and smaller and smaller, and some of them are actually detached from my organs now, which is great." He's feeling well enough that, in June, he's going to tackle the Epic1000 — a 1,000-km ride along the Trans Canada Trail. Nitsche estimates that it'll take about 12 to 14 days to complete. "It's not a race. You can just take your time, and, but there are other days where you feel good and go 160k or 140k," he explains. Dave Nitsche. Courtesy Dave Nitsche Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories. Now retired, Nitsche has turned to advocacy, leading his local chapter of the men's support group Man Up to Cancer. "People come up to me and they say, 'Oh, you've got cancer, well, you don't look like you have cancer.' And my reaction is always, 'Well, I'll try harder next time,' " Nitsche says jokingly. "It's a big misconception that you're on a bed and you can't do anything. We try to get out for walks with [the support group members] and get them moving. So that is a big, big misconception [that] you can't do anything." "You can," he says.
